messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: low frequency, mid load; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 680 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: high frequency, small Cp, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 17.5 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: low frequency, large Cp; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: high frequency, large Cp, heavy load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: hot, heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 200 kOhm, temperature 85 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2     simulation failed
S3        4.2    4.21    23.2  0.0865      3.75  ok       FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL    
S4       1.79    1.82    57.1   0.759      3.21  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       1.74    1.74    8.96       -      20.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6       1.55    1.56    25.4       -        12  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load $R_L$ from a piezo energy harvester.
    *   Output Requirements:
        *   $V_{avg} \ge 1.8$ V (at 0.7-0.8s)
        *   $V_{max} \le 3.6$ V (entire run)
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05$ V (at 0.7-0.8s)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4$ s (time to reach 1.8V)
        *   $dV \le 0.02$ V (stability between 0.6-0.7s and 0.7-0.8s)
    *   Piezo Model: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ || $C_p$ || 20 M$\Omega$ resistance.
    *   Open-circuit voltage amplitude $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p) \approx 3.2$ V at S1.
    *   Conditions: S1 to S6 (various $I_p, f, C_p, R_L$, and temp).
    *   Constraints: Max 16 components, specific parts (DSCH, DSI, DZ33, S, SYNC, R, C, L).

    *   Reference (FBR): Full-bridge rectifier.
    *   Failures: $V_{max}$ too high in S3 (4.2V), $V_{avg}$ too low in S4, S5, S6. Startup time too slow in S4.
    *   Key issue: FBR is passive. Low-frequency/heavy-load conditions (S4, S5, S6) struggle to provide enough power or reach the threshold quickly. High-frequency/light-load (S3) overshoots.

    *   To improve efficiency and startup, we need to extract more energy from the piezo capacitance $C_p$.
    *   Standard techniques:
        *   *SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):* Uses an inductor and a switch to invert the voltage on $C_p$ at the extrema, effectively "flipping" the charge and increasing the voltage available to the rectifier.
        *   *SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction):* Extracts charge at the peaks.
        *   *Buck-Boost/DC-DC:* Usually too complex for the given components (needs multiple SYNCs and a more complex topology).
    *   Given the components (SYNC, S, L, D), a modified SSHI or a simple inductor-based boost/charge-pump approach is feasible.

    *   **Design 1: SSHI-like (Parallel SSHI)**
        *   Concept: Use a switch and inductor to invert the piezo voltage at the peaks.
        *   Structure:
            *   Piezo nodes: `pzp`, `pzn`.
            *   Rectifier: Bridge (though a half-bridge might suffice if the inversion is perfect, but FBR is safer for stability). Actually, a simpler SSHI typically uses a switch and inductor across the piezo terminals to flip the voltage, then a rectifier to move charge to `out`.
            *   Components:
                *   Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo to flip $V_{pzp}-V_{pzn}$ at peaks.
                *   Rectifier (FBR) to get energy to `out`.
                *   Zener clamp (DZ33) to ensure $V_{max} \le 3.6$ V.
                *   Large storage capacitor $C_{out}$ on `out`.

    *   **Design 2: Simple Boost/Charge-Pump (L-C-S)**
        *   Concept: Instead of full FBR, use an inductor to step up the voltage.
        *   Since we have SYNC, we can do a basic switched-inductor circuit.
        *   Let's try a "Synchronous Rectification" style or a "charge extraction" circuit.
        *   Topology: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Inductor $\rightarrow$ Switch (to GND/return) $\rightarrow$ Diode $\rightarrow$ Out. (This is essentially the basic SSHI energy extraction).

    *   **Design 3: Modified Bridge with Zener Clamp and optimized C**
        *   Wait, FBR failed mainly on $V_{avg}$ and $V_{max}$.
        *   Adding a Zener diode (DZ33) to `out` handles $V_{max}$.
        *   But $V_{avg}$ in S5/S6 is low. FBR is inefficient because it doesn't account for $C_p$.
        *   A better approach is a "Parallel-SSHI" where the inductor-switch pair flips the voltage, then a bridge extracts it.

    *   Piezo: `pzp`, `pzn`.
    *   Inverter: $L_1$ and $S_1$ in parallel with the piezo. $S_1$ closes at peaks.
    *   Rectifier: 4 diodes (DSCH) - Bridge.
    *   Storage: $C_{out}$ on `out`.
    *   Protection: DZ33 on `out`.

    *Self-Correction on Inverter:* If I put $L_1$ and $S_1$ in parallel with the piezo, the energy flips between $C_p$ and $L_1$.
    Nodes: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ $L_1$ $\rightarrow$ node `n1` $\rightarrow$ $S_1$ $\rightarrow$ `pzn`.
    This is basically a parallel LC tank when $S_1$ is closed.

    *Rectifier Logic:*
    D1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
    D2: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out` (Wait, this is wrong for a bridge)
    Standard Bridge:
    D1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
    D2: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`
    D3: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp` (Wrong, anode on 0)
    D4: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn` (Wrong)
    Correct Bridge:
    D1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
    D2: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`
    D3: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp` (No, an anode on 0) $\rightarrow$ `pzp` is not correct.
    Actually, the reference FBR: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"].
    Wait, the reference says: "full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have their anode on ground)".
    Let's check:
    D1: pzp -> out
    D2: pzn -> out
    D3: 0 -> pzp (Wait, if pzp is negative, this conducts)
    D4: 0 -> pzn (If pzn is negative, this conducts)
    This is a standard full-bridge if the piezo is floating.

    *   S1: $V_{oc} \approx 3.2$ V.
    *   FBR $V_{avg} = 2.24$ V.
    *   S3: $V_{max} = 4.2$ V (Too high). DZ33 (3.3V) will cap this.
    *   S4: $V_{avg} = 1.79$ V (Too low). SSHI inversion helps.
    *   S5: $V_{avg} = 1.74$ V (Too low). SSHI inversion helps.
    *   S6: $V_{avg} = 1.55$ V (Too low). SSHI inversion helps.

    *   $L_1$ and $S_1$ flip the voltage.
    *   $L_1$ value: $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$. For $C_p=25\text{nF}$, $L=10\text{mH} \Rightarrow t_{on} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{10^{-2} \times 25 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 3.14 \times 1.58 \times 10^{-5} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.
    *   This fits the $1\mu\text{s}$ limit for $t_{on}$? NO!
    *   Wait: "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds (1e-07..0.001)".
    *   $0.001$ s is $1\text{ms}$. $50\mu\text{s}$ is well within $1\text{ms}$.

    *   Design A: SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener.
    *   Design B: SSHI + Half Bridge (Single diode to out) + Zener. (Might be too low voltage).
    *   Design C: A simpler buck-like structure if possible? No, let's stick to SSHI variations.

    Let's refine Design A (Parallel SSHI + FBR + Zener):
    - D1: pzp -> out (DSCH)
    - D2: pzn -> out (DSCH)
    - D3: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
    - D4: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
    - DZ1: 0 -> out (DZ33)
    - Cout: out -> 0 (e.g., 4.7uF)
    - L1: pzp -> n1 (e.g., 10mH)
    - S1: n1 -> pzn (ctrl: G1)
    - G1: SYNC (edges: both, phase: 0, ton: 50us)

    Wait, if $L_1$ and $S_1$ are in parallel with the piezo, they short the piezo. If $S_1$ is closed at the peak, the voltage flips.
    Let's double-check the nodes.
    Piezo is between `pzp` and `pzn`.
    `pzp` --- L1 --- `n1` --- S1 --- `pzn`.
    When S1 is closed, L1 is in parallel with (pzp-pzn). Correct.

    Does this conflict with the rectifier?
    The rectifier takes the voltage from `pzp` and `pzn`.
    When S1 is closed, the voltage across `pzp` and `pzn` is rapidly changing.
    This is the standard SSHI approach.

    Let's consider the $V_{max} \le 3.6$ V limit. DZ33 is 3.3 V. That's a good safety margin.
    $V_{avg} \ge 1.8$ V. SSHI should boost this.
    $t_{up} \le 0.4$ s. SSHI increases power extraction, speeding up startup.
    $V_{pp} \le 0.05$ V. A large $C_{out}$ should handle this.

    Can we simplify? Maybe a half-bridge is enough?
    If the piezo is balanced (pzp and pzn), a half-bridge only gets half the energy. FBR is better.

    Wait, the "Reference Design FBR" failed S3 on $V_{max}$ and S4, S5, S6 on $V_{avg}$.
    S3: $V_{max} = 4.2$ V. (A zener solves this).
    S4, S5, S6: $V_{avg} < 1.8$ V. (SSHI solves this).

    Let's try one more topology: "Series SSHI" or "SECE".
    SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction) usually uses a switch and an inductor to "pull" charge out at the peaks.
    Parallel SSHI is more common and generally more efficient for $V_{oc}$ around 3V.

    *Topology 1 (Parallel SSHI + Bridge + Zener):*
    - 4 Diodes (Bridge)
    - 1 Zener (Clamp)
    - 1 Capacitor (Storage)
    - 1 Inductor (Flip)
    - 1 Switch (Flip)
    - 1 SYNC (Control)
    Total = 9 components. Well within 16.

    *Topology 2 (Modified SSHI - maybe only one diode?):*
    If we use a SYNC to switch the piezo to the storage cap, we can avoid some diodes.
    But the Bridge is very robust. Let's try a different inductor placement.
    Instead of parallel, put the inductor in series with the rectifier. (Basically a boost converter).
    `pzp` $\rightarrow$ $L_1$ $\rightarrow$ `n1` $\rightarrow$ $D_{rect}$ $\rightarrow$ `out`.
    S1: `n1` $\rightarrow$ `pzn` (S1 closes to build energy in L1).
    This is a Boost converter.
    G1: SYNC (edges: "both", phase: 0, ton: 50us).
    This could be more efficient than SSHI for low $V_{oc}$.

    *Topology 3 (Parallel SSHI with lower-drop components):*
    Just a refinement of Topology 1.

    Let's refine the Boost approach (Topology 2) more:
    - L1: pzp -> n1
    - S1: n1 -> pzn (ctrl: G1)
    - D1: n1 -> out (DSCH)
    - C1: out -> 0
    - DZ1: 0 -> out (DZ33)
    - G1: SYNC (edges: both, ton: 50us)
    Wait, this only works when pzp is positive. For the negative cycle, we need another path.
    - L2: pzn -> n2
    - S2: n2 -> pzp (ctrl: G2)
    - D2: n2 -> out (DSCH)
    - G2: SYNC (edges: both, ton: 50us, phase: 0.5)
    This is a dual-boost.

    Let's stick with the most reliable one first: Parallel SSHI + FBR + Zener.

    Wait, look at the "Reference Design FBR" results again.
    S1: 2.24V (OK)
    S2: FAIL (Simulation failed)
    S3: 4.2V (Too high)
    S4: 1.79V (Too low)
    S5: 1.74V (Too low)
    S6: 1.55V (Too low)
    The failure in S2 (simulation failed) might be due to a very light load or numerical issues. $R_L$ is 680k.
    $V_{avg}$ is just below 1.8V in S4, S5. A small boost will fix it.

    One more check: The reference FBR had a 2.2uF capacitor.
    For $V_{pp} \le 0.05$ V, we might need a larger capacitor.
    $I_{load} = 1.8\text{V} / 150\text{k}\Omega = 12\mu\text{A}$.
    $\Delta V = I \cdot \Delta t / C$.
    Period $T = 1/100\text{Hz} = 10\text{ms}$.
    $\Delta V = 12\mu\text{A} \cdot 10\text{ms} / 2.2\mu\text{F} \approx 54\text{mV}$.
    This is right on the edge of $0.05$ V. Increasing $C_{out}$ to $4.7\mu\text{F}$ or $10\mu\text{F}$ would be safer.

    Final check on the SSHI Bridge:
    Components:
    - D1: pzp -> out
    - D2: pzn -> out
    - D3: 0 -> pzp
    - D4: 0 -> pzn
    - DZ1: 0 -> out (Zener clamp)
    - C1: out -> 0
    - L1: pzp -> n1
    - S1: n1 -> pzn
    - G1: SYNC (edges: both, phase: 0, ton: 50us)
    Total components: 9.

    Is there a risk with the SSHI switch $S_1$ being in parallel with the bridge?
    When $S_1$ is closed, the voltage across `pzp` and `pzn` is clamped to the inductor's behavior. The bridge will still function, but it will see the oscillating voltage. This is exactly how SSHI is supposed to work.

    Wait, if $S_1$ closes at the peak, it flips the voltage.
    If $V_{pzp} = 3\text{V}, V_{pzn} = 0\text{V}$, $S_1$ closes $\rightarrow$ $V_{pzp}$ becomes $-3\text{V}, V_{pzn}$ becomes $0\text{V}$ (roughly).
    The bridge:
    D1 (pzp->out) will be off.
    D3 (0->pzp) will be on.
    The energy is extracted during the "non-switching" phase.

    Let's try a second alternative: A "Charge Extraction" (SECE) circuit.
    SECE:
    - L1: pzp -> n1
    - S1: n1 -> out (ctrl: G1)
    - D1: pzp -> out (Wait, no)
    Actually, Parallel SSHI is more robust for these parameters.

    What about a "Synchronous Rectifier"?
    Replacing diodes with switches. But we only have 4 switches. FBR already uses 4 diodes.
    Let's provide a few variations of the SSHI.

    Variation 1: Parallel SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener (The "Gold Standard").
    Variation 2: Parallel SSHI + Half Bridge + Zener (More efficient, lower voltage).
    Variation 3: Inductor-based Boost + Zener (Dual-path).

    Wait, "Half Bridge" means only one diode. If the piezo is symmetric, $V_{pzp}$ goes from $-3$ to $3$. A half bridge (pzp $\rightarrow$ out) only collects the positive half. The negative half is wasted. Parallel SSHI flips the voltage, but the bridge is still the best way to collect it.

    Let's refine the Parallel SSHI nodes to be absolutely sure.
    Piezo is between `pzp` and `pzn`.
    Bridge:
    D1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `out`
    D2: `pzn` $\rightarrow$ `out`
    D3: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzp`
    D4: `0` $\rightarrow$ `pzn`
    S1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `pzn` (Wait, the prompt says $L$ has series resistance. I must use $L$).
    L1: `pzp` $\rightarrow$ `n1`
    S1: `n1` $\rightarrow$ `pzn`
    G1: SYNC (edges: both, phase: 0, ton: 50us)

    One detail: "phase shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation period (-0.25..0.25)".
    $0$ phase means it triggers at the zero crossings of the *current*.
    Zero crossing of current $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ is $t=0, T/2, T \dots$
    The *voltage* peaks are at these zero crossings of the current.
    So `phase: 0` is correct for triggering at voltage extrema.
